message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"3.36","text":"Nevertheless, if anyone surveys the whole accurately by reason, he will find that God has made it for the sake of humankind. For rainstorms occur for the sake of crops, so that a human may partake of them and animals may be fed so that they may serve humankind. The sun also shines and turns the air through four seasonal changes, so that each season may furnish humankind with what belongs to it. Springs also gush forth so that drink may be given to humans. Moreover, who, to the extent possible, exercises dominion over creation? Is it not the human being, who has received wisdom to cultivate the earth, sail the sea, hunt swimming creatures, flying creatures, and wild beasts, calculate the course of the stars, mine the earth, sift the sea, raise cities, appoint kings, establish laws, judge, conceive of an invisible God, know the names of angels, drive out demons, attempt to stop diseases with medicines, discover incantations against venomous reptiles, and devise natural counteragents?","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ πᾶν ἀκριβῶς λογισμῷ συνίδῃ","chosen":"surveys the whole accurately by reason","rationale":"τὸ πᾶν denotes the whole created order under consideration, while λογισμός indicates rational reflection."},{"source_quote":"τὸν ἀέρα εἰς τέσσαρας τροπὰς τρέπει","chosen":"turns the air through four seasonal changes","rationale":"The following reference to each καιρός supports understanding the four τροπαί as seasonal changes; “turns the air into four turnings” is the more literal alternative."},{"source_quote":"νηκτὰ πτηνὰ θηρία ἀγρεύειν","chosen":"hunt swimming creatures, flying creatures, and wild beasts","rationale":"The asyndetic accusatives name three classes of creatures subject to human hunting."},{"source_quote":"θάλασσαν σήθειν","chosen":"sift the sea","rationale":"σήθειν literally means to sift or strain; the unusual image of searching or working the sea is retained."},{"source_quote":"ἀντιπαθείας ἐπινοεῖν","chosen":"devise natural counteragents","rationale":"In the context of venomous reptiles, ἀντιπάθειαι are opposing properties or remedies; “devise antipathies” is a more literal but less intelligible alternative."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.37","text":"If you were grateful, human being, having recognized the God who benefited you in everything, you would also be immortal, with the things created for your sake possessing continued existence through gratitude. But even now you can become incorruptible, if you recognize the one you failed to notice, if you love the one you abandoned, and if you pray to him alone, who is able to punish and save your body and soul. Therefore, above all, consider that no one rules together with him and no one shares his designation—namely, that which is called “God.” For he alone is both called God and is God, and it is permitted neither to regard another as God nor to call another God. If anyone should dare to do so, that person’s soul is destined to be punished eternally.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"εἰ δὲ εὐγνωμόνεις","chosen":"If you were grateful","rationale":"The imperfect with ἂν ἦς forms a counterfactual condition; εὐγνωμονεῖν here denotes gratitude or proper acknowledgment toward a benefactor."},{"source_quote":"τῶν διὰ σὲ κτισθέντων δι’ εὐγνωμοσύνην τὸ διαμένειν ἐχόντων","chosen":"with the things created for your sake possessing continued existence through gratitude","rationale":"The Greek does not expressly identify whose εὐγνωμοσύνη is meant, so the main wording leaves its possessor unstated. It may refer to the human addressee’s gratitude within the hypothetical condition, or to the created things’ own gratitude or good disposition, in which case their continuance supplies the comparison underlying “you would also be immortal.”"},{"source_quote":"ἐὰν ἐπιγνῷς ὃν ἔλαθες","chosen":"if you recognize the one you failed to notice","rationale":"The context contrasts recognizing God with previously abandoning him and supports the extended sense “failed to notice” or “overlooked.” The ordinary active construction of λανθάνω with an accusative can instead mean “the one whose notice you escaped”; that materially different reading remains grammatically possible, though it fits the immediate theological argument less readily."},{"source_quote":"οὐδεὶς τῆς αὐτοῦ κοινωνεῖ ὀνομασίας","chosen":"no one shares his designation","rationale":"ὀνομασία denotes the designation or name subsequently identified as “God.”"},{"source_quote":"ἄλλον δὲ οὔτε νομίσαι οὔτε εἰπεῖν ἔξεστιν","chosen":"it is permitted neither to regard another as God nor to call another God","rationale":"The preceding discussion supplies “God” as the complement of both verbs; νομίζειν can also be rendered “acknowledge” or “consider.”"},{"source_quote":"ἀιδίως τὴν ψυχὴν κολασθῆναι ἔχει","chosen":"that person’s soul is destined to be punished eternally","rationale":"ἔχει with the infinitive expresses an impending or necessary consequence rather than possession."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.38","text":"When Peter had said these things, Simon, from outside the crowd, said in a loud voice, “Why do you wish, by lying, to deceive the uninstructed crowd standing by you, persuading it that it is permitted neither to regard any as gods nor to call them gods, when the public books among the Jews say that there are many gods? And now, moreover, together with everyone, I wish to debate with you from those very books about the need to acknowledge gods. But first I will demonstrate that the god of whom you spoke is not the highest power capable of everything, since he lacks foreknowledge, is incomplete, is needy, is not good, and is subject to many—indeed, countless—painful passions. Consequently, when this has been demonstrated from the Scriptures, as I maintain, there remains another, unattested in writing, who possesses foreknowledge, is perfect, needs nothing, is good, and is free from all painful passions. But the one whom you call the Creator proves to be subject to the opposites.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἰδιώτην ὄχλον","chosen":"uninstructed crowd","rationale":"ἰδιώτης here characterizes the crowd as lacking specialist knowledge; “ordinary crowd” or “lay crowd” are possible alternatives."},{"source_quote":"θεοὺς μήτε νομίζειν μήτε λέγειν","chosen":"neither to regard any as gods nor to call them gods","rationale":"νομίζειν concerns acknowledgment or recognition, while λέγειν concerns naming or speaking of them as gods."},{"source_quote":"τῶν παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις δημοσίων βίβλων","chosen":"the public books among the Jews","rationale":"δημόσιοι presents the books as public or commonly recognized; “canonical books” would introduce a later technical category."},{"source_quote":"καὶ νῦν δὲ μετὰ πάντων","chosen":"And now, moreover, together with everyone","rationale":"μετὰ πάντων expresses association with everyone. It may portray everyone as participating in the discussion or, contextually, indicate that the debate occurs with everyone present; the Greek does not explicitly choose between those attachments."},{"source_quote":"περὶ τοῦ δεῖν θεοὺς νομίζειν","chosen":"about the need to acknowledge gods","rationale":"The articular infinitive presents the necessity of acknowledging gods as the subject for discussion; it does not itself introduce an open question about whether that necessity exists."},{"source_quote":"ἀπρόγνωστός ἐστιν","chosen":"he lacks foreknowledge","rationale":"The active sense is favored by the explicit contrast with προγνωστικός and by the following accusations of ignorance. The adjective can also be read formally as passive, “he is not known beforehand,” but that reading fits the stated contrast less directly."},{"source_quote":"ἕτερος ἀγράφως περιλείπεται εἶναι","chosen":"there remains another, unattested in writing","rationale":"ἀγράφως may mean that this other deity is unattested in writing or that the deity is inferred apart from written accounts; the former is adopted in the main text."},{"source_quote":"πολλοῖς καὶ μυρίοις χαλεποῖς ὑποκείμενος πάθεσιν","chosen":"subject to many—indeed, countless—painful passions","rationale":"The rendering preserves both πολλοῖς and the intensifying μυρίοις, while πάθη can denote passions, experienced states, or afflictions."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.39","text":"For example, Adam, who came into being according to his likeness, is created blind, is handed down as possessing no knowledge of good or evil, is found to be a transgressor, is expelled from Paradise, and is punished with death. Likewise, the one who formed him, since he does not see from every direction, says at the destruction of Sodom, “Come, and after going down let us see whether they are carrying matters through in accordance with their outcry that is coming to me; but if not, so that I may know,” and thereby shows himself to be ignorant. As for his saying about Adam, “Let us cast him out, lest perhaps, after stretching out his hand, he touch the tree of life and eat, and he will live forever”—his saying “lest perhaps” indicates ignorance, while his addition, “lest perhaps, after eating, he live forever,” also indicates envy. That it is written, “God considered that he had made the human being,” means that he both changes his mind and is ignorant. For “considered” is a reflection by which someone, through ignorance, wishes to determine precisely the outcome of what he intends, or the reflection of someone regretting something that did not turn out according to his intention. That it is written, “And the Lord smelled an odor of fragrance,” belongs to one who is needy, while taking pleasure in the fatty smoke of flesh belongs to one who is not good. Testing—as it is written, “And the Lord tested Abraham”—belongs to one who is evil and ignorant of the outcome of the endurance.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"γνῶσιν ἀγαθοῦ ἢ κακοῦ οὐκ ἔχων παραδέδοται","chosen":"is handed down as possessing no knowledge of good or evil","rationale":"The perfect passive παραδέδοται can describe how Adam is transmitted or represented in the received account; “is delivered over while possessing no knowledge” is possible but less coherent in this sequence."},{"source_quote":"ἐπεὶ μὴ πανταχόθεν βλέπει","chosen":"since he does not see from every direction","rationale":"The literal spatial image of πανταχόθεν is retained rather than replaced with the interpretive abstraction “is not omniscient.”"},{"source_quote":"τὸ εἰπεῖν „μήπως“ ἀγνοεῖ","chosen":"his saying “lest perhaps” indicates ignorance","rationale":"When Simon isolates μήπως, he treats its expression of apprehension or uncertainty as evidence of ignorance. The word can be represented contextually by “lest,” while “perhaps” makes explicit the uncertainty on which his argument depends."},{"source_quote":"τὸ δὲ ἐπαγαγεῖν „μήπως φαγὼν ζήσεται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα“ καὶ φθονεῖ","chosen":"while his addition, “lest perhaps, after eating, he live forever,” also indicates envy","rationale":"In the repeated clause μήπως retains its apprehensive and preventive force, connecting Adam’s possible eating and living forever with the accusation of envy; rendering it merely “perhaps” would obscure that connection."},{"source_quote":"καὶ μετανοεῖ καὶ ἀγνοεῖ","chosen":"he both changes his mind and is ignorant","rationale":"Here μετανοεῖ denotes alleged divine reconsideration or regret, not moral-spiritual reorientation toward God."},{"source_quote":"κνίσῃ σαρκῶν","chosen":"the fatty smoke of flesh","rationale":"κνίση is the steam, smoke, or savor produced by burning fat or flesh; the rendering retains the polemically physical image."},{"source_quote":"τὸ τέλος τῆς ὑπομονῆς","chosen":"the outcome of the endurance","rationale":"τέλος can denote either the outcome or the limit of endurance; “outcome” best fits the claim that testing seeks information about the eventual result."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"πρὸς μὲ","issue":"The printed grave accent on μὲ is an apparent accentuation irregularity. The context clearly calls for the first-person pronoun “me,” so the wording remains translatable without supplying missing content.","proposed_reading":"πρὸς με","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"3.40","text":"Similarly, Simon seemed to show from many things in the Scriptures that God is subject to every passion. In response Peter said, “If an evil and utterly wicked person does not at all wish to expose himself regarding the things in which he sins, answer me.” Simon said, “He does not wish to.” Peter said, “How, then, can God be evil and wicked, if it was by his own will that the evils publicly written against him were added?” Simon replied, “It is possible that, contrary to his intention, the exposure against him was written by another power.” Peter said, “First, then, let us investigate this. If he exposed himself by his own counsel, as you just agreed, he is not wicked. But if it was done by another power, the matter must be investigated—and with all our strength. It must be examined whether someone has subjected him, though he is nothing but good, to all the evil things.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὁμῶς","chosen":"Similarly","rationale":"ὁμῶς can mean “likewise” or “in the same way,” linking the summary to Simon’s preceding examples."},{"source_quote":"μηδὲν ἀγαπᾷ ... ἑαυτὸν ἐλέγχειν","chosen":"does not at all wish to expose himself","rationale":"ἀγαπᾷ with the infinitive concerns willingness or desire, while ἐλέγχειν here means exposing or convicting one’s own wrongdoing."},{"source_quote":"αὐτοῦ λείμματι","chosen":"by his own will","rationale":"The immediate contrast with παρὰ προαίρεσιν αὐτοῦ and ὑπὸ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ βουλῆς supports interpreting the printed λείμματι as an orthographic form of λήματι from λῆμα, “will” or “resolve.” The ordinary sense of λείμμα, “remainder, deficiency, or omission,” does not readily sustain Peter’s argument."},{"source_quote":"τὸν κατ’ αὐτοῦ γραφῆναι ἔλεγχον","chosen":"the exposure against him was written","rationale":"ἔλεγχος can mean refutation, censure, conviction, or exposure; “exposure” preserves the connection with God’s alleged disclosure of blameworthy traits."},{"source_quote":"αὐτὸν μόνον ἀγαθὸν ὄντα","chosen":"though he is nothing but good","rationale":"The main rendering takes μόνον adverbially with ἀγαθόν, emphasizing the absence of evil in God; this is favored by the immediate contrast with the charges that he is evil and wicked. Because μόνον agrees formally with αὐτόν, it can instead mean “though he alone is good,” excluding goodness from others; the surrounding insistence on divine uniqueness supports that alternative."},{"source_quote":"μή τις αὐτὸν μόνον ἀγαθὸν ὄντα ἐπὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς κακοῖς ὑπέβαλεν","chosen":"whether someone has subjected him, though he is nothing but good, to all the evil things","rationale":"μή introduces the matter to be examined, while ὑποβάλλειν ἐπί can mean subjecting someone to adverse things, accusations, or representations."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"λείμματι","issue":"The confirmed printed form ordinarily points to λείμμα, “remainder, deficiency, or omission,” but the immediate contrasts with “contrary to his intention” and “by his own counsel” strongly suggest an orthographic form of λήματι from λῆμα, “will” or “resolve.” This interpretation remains a contextual proposal rather than a silent alteration of the selected edition.","proposed_reading":"λήματι","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
